title: Chapter 137 – A Brother's Fire
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Feng]

Seven years later.

Lin Feng is sixty-four years old, and his brother has been going up the ridge once a month for as long as he can remember.

It is a quiet ritual. On the last night of every moon, at dusk, Jian takes his cloak and walks out of the Garden gate with nothing in his hands. He goes up the long cold stair behind the Sutra Hall, through the web of the Keeping, to the door of the ridge-house, and there a veiled man in plum-colored gauze lets him in. He is gone until dawn. In the morning he comes down gray-faced and slow, with his hair a little whiter than when he left, and sits in the kitchen with a bowl of porridge that his mother cannot taste, and says nothing.

Feng walks him to the foot of the stair every time. He carries a staff. He does not offer to go in.

It is the arrangement. It was made in the autumn of the year Jian came back from the Court, in a long cold hour across a table in the Hall of Elders, between a gray farmer's son and a veiled stranger who did not give his name. The terms were simple. Jian would hold the Chain: sit with the thirty sleepers one night a month, lend them his breath, steady the rope that was fraying at their ankles. In exchange the Second House would not touch the Garden, the Gate, the Sutra Hall, the Court or the Seat. Neither would the Numbers. Neither would the clerks.

"For how long?" Wuping had asked.

"Until I find a better way," Jian had said.

Seven years. Feng has counted them, one moon at a time. Eighty-four nights.

He has never once seen his brother complain.

* * *

On the eighty-fourth night, he sees the Warden.

It is the last night of the moon, and a thin cold rain is falling. Feng stands at the foot of the ridge-house stair in his oilcloth cloak with the staff planted in the mud, watching his brother's gray shape climb the steps into the dark. Halfway up, Jian stops and turns, and lifts one hand. Feng lifts his own. Then the rain closes in and the figure is gone.

He waits. It is his habit. He stands in the rain for an hour, then two, with the water running down his neck, and nobody comes to move him on. The Second House's clerks have learned that it is easier to leave Lin Feng alone. They bring him a lantern, once, and a cup of tea. He does not drink it. He sets it on a rock to cool.

At the third watch a tall figure comes down the stair.

It is veiled, in plum-colored gauze, with a long sword at its hip. It descends slowly, one step at a time, with a hand on the rail. Feng has seen it before, from a distance. He knows what it is. A Golden Core cultivator can crush a Foundation Late man between two fingers, and he has never once felt anything from this one but a heavy, patient, bone-deep exhaustion.

It stops three steps above him.

"Elder Lin," says the Warden.

"Warden."

"It is a cold night."

"It is the usual sort." Feng does not lower the staff. "He is well?"

"He is sleeping." The veil does not move. "I sat with him for an hour. He did not wake. He lay on the jade among the others with his eyes shut and his hands folded, breathing in their time, and the thirty sleepers did not stir. It is a thing I have not seen in a dozen years. The Chain is quiet when he is with it."

"I know."

"Do you?" The voice is level, dry, tired. There is something wrong in it, something Feng cannot name, like a bell struck in an empty house. "I wonder sometimes whether any of you know. What it costs him. What it costs me, to stand there and watch." A pause. "I used to be a man who knew exactly what he wanted."

"What did you want?"

"I cannot remember." The Warden lifts a hand to the veil, almost touching it, and lets the hand drop. "That is a poor joke. Forgive me. I am not accustomed to company."

Feng is silent. The rain hisses on the stone.

"I knew you," he says slowly. "Before. There was a man who carried a sword on the north terrace of Cloud Peak. He had a way of standing, as though the whole world were beneath him, and he was only waiting for it to apologize." He watches the veil. "You have his shoulders."

For a very long moment, nothing.

"Do I?" says the Warden, quite softly.

"Yes."

"Thank you." The tall figure inclines its head. "I find that I like to be told."

It goes down the stair past him, and into the dark.

* * *

The Garden at dawn is the loveliest place in the world, and he thinks so every morning.

He stands on the practice yard in the gray light with a staff in his hands and forty young men in front of him, in rows, in sweat-darkened shirts. The yard is a wide trampled square of earth at the top of the lower terrace, and beyond it the whole valley drops away in tiers of green and gold. A mist lies in the hollows. A cock crows. From the long low shed behind him comes the smell of baking.

"Again," he says.

They go through the form. It is the plain old Garden form, thirty-six movements, taught by Hu to Feng and by Feng to a hundred others. It has no name. It has no secrets. It is a way of standing and a way of striking and a way of not falling over, and a boy can learn the whole of it in a month. Feng has taught it for thirty-five years.

"Lower, Chen. Your hip."

"Yes, Uncle."

"Do not say Yes, Uncle. Move the hip."

The boy moves it. Feng nods. He is a Foundation Establishment Late cultivator, broad and slow and gray in the beard, with a scarred left hand and a bad knee, and he has been stuck at the same step for nineteen years. He has long since stopped being ashamed of it. A man can stand on a stair for a very long time and still be of use to the people below.

The pill sits in his mind like a stone. He does not think about it often.

"Uncle Feng." It is a thin, quiet voice at his elbow. He looks round. Yue's eldest, a serious boy of sixteen named Lin Zhao, is standing there with a ledger under his arm. "Mother says to come to the Hall. Uncle Jian has asked for you."

"Now?"

"She said, now, and then she said, bring the staff, and then she looked at the sky."

Feng grunts. When Yue looks at the sky it means somebody is about to say something important. He hands the staff to Chen, wipes his hands on his leggings, and goes.

* * *

The Hall is full.

He had not expected that. Every seat at the long table is taken: his father, eighty-four and silver, in a thick scarf and lined gloves; his mother, who looks fifty and has no business doing so; Yue; Hu, a bent gray man with two bronze arms; the Garden's elders; Zhao Yao, who walks with a cane now; even old Wenqing, carried in a chair. And at the head of the table, standing, with his hands flat on the wood and a jar in front of him, is Jian.

He has changed. Feng sees it at once. He is fifty-eight, and his hair has gone entirely white, a clean even silver, brushed back from a high lined forehead. His face is thin. His eyes, when they meet Feng's, are very bright and very tired, as though the lids had been propped open with matchsticks. He is wearing the plain gray cloak he has worn for thirty years, and he is, Feng realizes, standing very straight, in the way a man stands when he is afraid of what will happen if he sits.

"Elder Brother," he says. "Thank you for coming."

"You called."

"I did." He lifts the jar. It is squat and black and sealed with wax. "Do you remember what I told you, when you were forty-three, and I was thirty-seven?"

"That I would break through."

"That you would break through. Not that day. But that when the day came, you would be ready." His smile is faint. "I am sorry it took so long."

Feng looks at the jar. He does not breathe.

"It is the Fire," says Jian. "The last reagent. Seven, you remember? Silver-thread, ember coral, Starfurnace ash, moon dew, southern fire-orchid, my blood three times, and the Fire. I used the Gate's Fire for myself. It was fed by the sleepers, and I will not use it again." He turns the jar in his hands. "This is another. A Fire that the fourth Operator kept for me in a school at the end of the world. It burns without breath. It does not need a sleeper. It costs nothing but itself."

"Jian—"

"It is yours."

The room is utterly silent. Zhao Yao, by the wall, has taken off his hat. Little Bell, Yue's youngest, nine years old, with a gap in her teeth and her mother's unblinking eyes, whispers loudly to a cousin, "Is Uncle Feng going to be a god?" and is shushed by three adults at once.

"I have been carrying it for nine years," says Jian. "I was waiting until I had the rest. I have the rest. Yao found the coral. Qinghe grew the thread. Ruyan sent the orchid from the south. Bai's jar of ash was in the Pill Hall. And the bench..." He swallows. "The bench has ninety CE in it. I have been saving them."

"For me."

"For you."

"You are mad," says Feng, hoarsely. "You should have used them on yourself."

"I have used what I need." His brother looks at him steadily. "You taught me to hold a staff, Feng. You taught me where to put my feet. For thirty-five years you have stood at the foot of every stair I have ever climbed, and you have never once asked me for a thing. I cannot give you the world. I can give you this."

Feng opens his mouth. He closes it. Somewhere at the back of the hall, a chair scrapes, and his mother makes a small hard sound, like a woman who has been holding her breath since the morning of the world.

"Well," says Feng, at last. His voice is not steady. "I suppose I had better not waste it."

* * *

It takes ten days to print the pill.

He does not watch. The Dock is a place he has never liked, a cold green cave beneath the Gate stair, humming faintly, with a smell like a struck match. He sits in the antechamber with Hu, drinking tea. Hu sits very upright, with his bronze hands on his knees, and does not speak. The old refiner has made the crucible with his own hands, a delicate thing of pale gray metal no bigger than a teacup, and he has cast, chiseled, polished and recast it eleven times. He will not say what it cost him.

On the tenth night Jian comes out.

He walks with his hand on the wall. In the other he carries a small clear box, and in the box, on a bed of white silk, lies a pill the color of a violet sunrise, smaller than a pea, pulsing very faintly with a light that seems to come from underneath. He sets it in Feng's palm. It is warm. It weighs nothing.

"Seven weeks," he says. "In the cocoon. Not more. If you wake early, the Fire burns your Qi. If you wake late, it burns your marrow."

"How will I know?"

"Yue will ring a bell." He sways. Feng catches him. He is shockingly light. "Forgive me. I have not slept in four days."

"You will sleep now."

"I will." His brother's smile is brief, crooked, entirely youthful. "I am only afraid I will dream of the sleepers."

Feng looks at the pill. Then at his brother's white head, bent against his shoulder. Then at the old refiner, who has risen from his bench and is regarding them both with a face as seamed and solemn as a mountain.

"Go on," says Hu gruffly. "Take it. The child's about to fall over."

He takes it.

* * *

Hu comes to see him the evening after the pill is printed, with a bundle under his arm and a face like a locked door.

He sits on the edge of Feng's bed and unwraps the bundle on his knees. It is a short staff, perhaps four feet long, of dark red wood, bound at both ends with bronze and inlaid along its length with a pattern so fine that it looks like a trail of ants. He turns it in his hands. In the lamplight, the inlay glimmers faintly.

"I made it in the winter," he says. "I did not know whether I would give it to you. I thought, if the pill failed, it would be a poor kind of gift. And if it succeeded, you would not need it." He shrugs one bronze shoulder. "I have never been good at timing."

"Hu."

"It is Dock steel in the ferrules. Jian printed me the blanks. The core is ironwood from the Orchard, from the last tree he found standing. He said you might want something to hold when the sounds got loud." Hu's voice roughens. "A man needs a thing to lean on, when the whole world begins to ring."

Feng takes the staff. It is lighter than he expects. Warm. When he closes his hand around it the faint high humming in the walls seems to dim a little, as though a hand had been laid over a bell.

"It dampens," he says, astonished.

"A little. I tried five times. It is not a cure." Hu gets heavily to his feet. "You were the first friend I had in this Garden, you know. Not Wenyuan. Wenyuan was the master. You were the boy who carried my bellows and never once asked why I drank."

"You were a good teacher."

"I was a very bad one." The old refiner pats the bed, twice, awkwardly. "But I had a very good pupil."

He goes out. Feng sits for a long time with the staff across his knees, listening to the Garden, and for the first time in his life he thinks that he may not mind the noise.

* * *

The night before the pill, his mother cooks him dinner and does not taste a bite of it.

She stands at the stove in the big Garden kitchen, in her apron, with her iron-gray braid pinned up, and stirs a pot of lentils with the focus of a woman defusing a bomb. Feng sits at the table with his hands folded. Wenyuan is across from him in his chair, with a bowl of tea and his gloves on. The younger grandchildren have been banished upstairs. The fire crackles. Outside, the first stars are coming out above the valley, hard and white.

"You are not to be nervous," says Qinghe, without turning.

"I am not."

"You are cracking your knuckles."

"I am stretching."

"You are cracking them." She tastes the pot, from long habit, and her face does not change, because she tastes nothing. She adds salt anyway, a measured pinch. "I carried you for nine months, Lin Feng. I know what you look like when you are nervous."

"I looked nervous?"

"You kicked." She ladles the lentils into three bowls. "A great deal."

Wenyuan makes a small dry sound that might be a laugh. Qinghe sets a bowl in front of each of them. She sits. She folds her hands.

"Eat," she says.

They eat. Nobody speaks. The lentils are very slightly scorched and over-salted, and Feng has never in his life enjoyed a meal more. When the bowls are empty Qinghe rises, and comes round the table, and puts her small strong hand on his gray head.

"I am so proud of you," she says, in a very quiet voice. "I have never said it. I should have, more often. You were the first. You were the one who taught me how to be a mother. I did it badly. I was frightened every day."

"Mother—"

"Hush. Let me finish." Her fingers tighten in his hair. "You have been a wall to this family for sixty-four years. You were a wall when you were six and your father was ill. You were a wall when the Orchard fell. You have been a wall for your brother, and your sister, and your children, and mine. I have never once seen you ask for anything." She bends and kisses the top of his head, hard. "Take it, Feng. Take what he is giving you. It is not charity. It is a debt."

He cannot speak. He nods, and she pats his shoulder, and goes back to the stove, and wipes her eyes on her apron with a noisy sniff, and says to the lentils that she has never in her life met a draft she could trust.

* * *

It is not like dying.

That is the first thing he notices. He lies on the mat in the dark room with the lamp turned low, in his shirt, with Qinghe's quilt up to his chin, and swallows the tiny pill like a man taking medicine. For a moment, nothing. Then the fire arrives, and it is not a burning at all, but a kind of vast, slow, brilliant opening, as if a window had been thrown wide in a room he had not known was shuttered.

He sees the whole of his life.

It does not pass before him. It stands, all at once, in a great quiet field: the Orchard in spring; his father's cold hands; a village girl he almost married and did not; Hu's hammer; a thousand dawns on the practice yard. A tall, quiet, odd little boy who looked at the lamp. He sees himself picking that boy up, at six, from the bottom of a ditch he had fallen into, and carrying him home on his back in the rain. You are heavy, he had said. I know, said the boy. I'm sorry.

Little brother, he thinks. You were never heavy. I only said so to hear you answer.

The fire deepens. He feels his bones grow light and his breath go wide. He feels the wall of his Foundation, that stubborn gray ceiling he has pushed against for nineteen years, dissolve like salt in water, and beyond it, a vast room full of light.

Purple Mansion, says some part of him. Is that all?

It is not all. It is the beginning of something very large. He floats in it for weeks, or hours. He hears, from a great distance, the sound of a bell ringing, once, softly. And then another. And then another, slower and louder, and something in him loosens like a fist, and he opens his eyes.

* * *

The room is full of voices.

He sits up. He is wet with sweat, and his hands tremble, and he is, for an instant, quite sure that he is going to be sick. Then the lamp comes into focus, and the quilt, and the plain wooden walls, and his sister's face, white and strained, bending over him with the bell in her hand.

"Seven weeks," says Yue. "To the hour."

"I did not feel it."

"No. You wouldn't." She sits back on her heels. Her eyes are bright and wet. "How do you feel?"

"Like I could carry the mountain on my back."

"Don't."

"I won't." He laughs. It comes out huge, a bellow that startles the lamp, and a dozen voices in the corridor outside cheer. "Purple Mansion. By all the old gods. Early. At sixty-four."

"Feng." Yue's voice is quiet. "Do you hear it?"

"Hear what?"

"The house."

He stops laughing.

He listens. At first there is nothing, only the creak of the beams, the muted scrape of a broom somewhere outside. Then, as though a veil had been drawn back, there comes a rush: a great soft swelling hum, from every wall and every floor and every board, thousands of tiny clear notes, ringing and ringing, each its own pitch, each its own place. A door in the kitchen, a hundred paces away, gives out a thin high ting. A window latch. A nail in a rafter. A knot in a plank. The very floor beneath him thrums with its own faint bright pulse.

Seams, he thinks. Each of them a place where two things meet and do not quite fit.

He claps his hands over his ears. It does no good. It is not outside.

"It will pass," says Yue. "A little. You learn to turn it down." She puts her hand on his arm. "I am sorry. I did not know it would reach you, too."

"It is the price."

"I think so. I think the Fire of the fourth Operator is a Fire that listens."

"I will not sleep."

"Not much." She tries to smile. "But you will always know when someone is at the door."

He lowers his hands, slowly. The hum is still there, bright and relentless, a whole world of tiny sounds. He thinks of his brother, who has lived with it for years, and has never once spoken of it. He thinks of Yue, with her book of doors and her tired eyes. He thinks of Pebble.

"Well," he says. His voice is shaky. "I always wished to be the wall."

"You are." Yue's grip tightens. "You were always the wall."

* * *

He finds Jian in the kitchen at dawn, eating porridge.

It is the first morning he has been able to walk. He goes slowly, with a hand on the doorframe, and every board under his foot sings. His brother is at the long table with his back to the window, in his shirtsleeves, with a bowl in front of him and a wooden spoon in his fist. Beyond the glass the valley is pearl and gold.

He sits. Jian pushes a second bowl toward him.

"Eat."

"I am not hungry."

"Eat anyway." His brother's voice is gentle. "It is not very good. Mother is making it."

Feng picks up the spoon. The porridge is thin and slightly burned. He eats it all.

"I wanted to say something," he says at last.

"Say it."

"I thought I was jealous." He studies the bowl. "For thirty years. You went up the stair and I stayed on the step. I thought, he is the one the world was made for, and I am the one who carries the bags." He swallows. "I lay in the fire for seven weeks and I understood that it was the other way round. You are the one who carries the bags. I only held the door."

"Feng—"

"Let me finish." His eyes are wet. "You will go up the stair again. I know it. The Core, the long seclusion. You will go where I cannot follow. And I want you to know that I will be at the bottom. Whatever comes. With my staff. With my ears full of doors." He lifts his head. "You will not have to look back to know I am there."

Jian does not answer. He sets down his spoon and looks at his brother for a long time. Then, quite slowly, he reaches across the table and lays his hand over Feng's, and the two of them sit like that in the gray light, two old men with spoons, while the mist burns off the valley.

"There is something else," says Jian, at last.

"Yes?"

"I have been listening, too." He turns his head toward the window. "Since you woke. I could not help it. When the ears open, one hears the others."

"What do you hear?"

"A voice." His brother's face has gone very still. "Far off. In the Sutra Hall. Reading. Over and over, in the oldest script. One name after another." He closes his eyes. "She has been at it for twenty-two years. And I think, Feng, that she is nearly finished."

Feng listens.

Far off, down the long chiming dark of the Garden's seams, past the kitchen door and the mill and the bell tower and the Gate stair, there comes a thin old voice, steady as a pendulum. A woman's voice, dry and clear and unhurried, reading a name. A pause. Another. A pause. He cannot make out the words. He can only hear the rhythm, the patient, endless, impossible rhythm of a person who has been giving back the dead for twenty-two years, one syllable at a time.

And under it, deeper, from the ridge, a different sound begins.

A groan. A long slow shifting sigh, like a very large animal turning over in its sleep.

Jian opens his eyes.

"It has noticed," he says.
